claim: Tuberculosis kills over 1.8 million people each year.
source: The past decade has seen the emergence of new diagnostics and drugs for tuberculosis, a disease that kills over 1.8 million people each year.
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion in the abstract and is consistent with established epidemiological data on TB mortality.

claim: New TB diagnostics have emerged on the market in the past decade.
source: Several new TB diagnostics have emerged on the market and many have also been policy-endorsed by WHO and other agencies (Pai and Schito, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pai and Schito, 2015.

claim: Xpert® MTB/RIF is a new TB diagnostic that has been policy-endorsed by WHO.
source: These new diagnostics include Xpert® MTB/RIF (Cepheid Inc, Sunnyvale, California) (World Health Organization, 2013a)
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2013a.

claim: Line probe assays are new TB diagnostics that have been policy-endorsed by WHO.
source: These new diagnostics include Xpert® MTB/RIF (Cepheid Inc, Sunnyvale, California) (World Health Organization, 2013a), line probe assays (World Health Organization, 2016b)
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2016b.

claim: Urine lipoarabinomannan antigen detection test is a new TB diagnostic that has been policy-endorsed by WHO.
source: These new diagnostics include Xpert® MTB/RIF (Cepheid Inc, Sunnyvale, California) (World Health Organization, 2013a), line probe assays (World Health Organization, 2016b), urine lipoarabinomannan antigen detection test (World Health Organization, 2015a)
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2015a.

claim: Liquid cultures are new TB diagnostics that have been policy-endorsed by WHO.
source: These new diagnostics include Xpert® MTB/RIF (Cepheid Inc, Sunnyvale, California) (World Health Organization, 2013a), line probe assays (World Health Organization, 2016b), urine lipoarabinomannan antigen detection test (World Health Organization, 2015a), liquid cultures (World Health Organization, 2007)
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2007.

claim: Interferon-gamma release assays are new TB diagnostics that have been policy-endorsed by WHO.
source: These new diagnostics include Xpert® MTB/RIF (Cepheid Inc, Sunnyvale, California) (World Health Organization, 2013a), line probe assays (World Health Organization, 2016b), urine lipoarabinomannan antigen detection test (World Health Organization, 2015a), liquid cultures (World Health Organization, 2007), and interferon-gamma release assays (World Health Organization, 2014a).
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2014a.

claim: An estimated 41% of the 10.4 million new TB cases globally are either undiagnosed or not reported.
source: This is underscored by the fact that an estimated 41% of the 10.4 million new cases globally are either undiagnosed or not reported (World Health Organization, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2016a providing epidemiological data.

claim: 4.3 million people with TB are 'missing' (undiagnosed or not reported).
source: These "missing" 4.3 million people with TB contribute to ongoing TB transmission, including the transmission of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB).
evidence: This is calculated from the 41% of 10.4 million cases mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Missing TB cases contribute to ongoing TB transmission, including transmission of multidrug-resistant TB.
source: These "missing" 4.3 million people with TB contribute to ongoing TB transmission, including the transmission of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on epidemiological principles that undiagnosed/untreated cases continue to transmit disease.

claim: Nearly 75% of the 480,000 cases of MDR-TB are either not detected or not reported.
source: Nearly 75% of the 480,000 cases of MDR-TB are either not detected or not reported (World Health Organization, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2016a providing epidemiological data.

claim: Nearly 40% of previously treated TB patients at risk of drug-resistance and mortality are not tested for drug resistance.
source: Even among previously treated patients at risk of drug-resistance and mortality, nearly 40% are not tested for drug resistance.
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion about testing practices, likely derived from WHO or other epidemiological sources.

claim: As of 31 December 2016, over 6,500 GeneXpert machines had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing.
source: Cumulatively, since the launch of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in 2010, over 6,500 GeneXpert machines and 23 million Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing, as of 31 December 2016 (World Health Organization, 2017a; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2017a and Figure 1 showing procurement data.

claim: As of 31 December 2016, 23 million Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing.
source: Cumulatively, since the launch of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in 2010, over 6,500 GeneXpert machines and 23 million Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing, as of 31 December 2016 (World Health Organization, 2017a; Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2017a and Figure 1 showing procurement data.

claim: The Xpert MTB/RIF assay was launched in 2010.
source: Cumulatively, since the launch of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in 2010, over 6,500 GeneXpert machines and 23 million Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing, as of 31 December 2016 (World Health Organization, 2017a; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion about the launch date.

claim: Over 77 million sputum smears are performed annually in 22 of the highest TB burden countries, including follow-up tests.
source: It is estimated that over 77 million sputum smears are performed annually in 22 of the highest TB burden countries, including follow-up tests (Kik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kik et al., 2014.

claim: South Africa accounts for almost 50% of global Xpert MTB/RIF volumes.
source: With the notable exception of South Africa, which has rolled-out Xpert MTB/RIF on a national scale and accounts for almost 50% of global Xpert MTB/RIF volumes, other countries are still reliant on insensitive smears (FIND et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to FIND et al., 2015.

claim: South Africa has rolled-out Xpert MTB/RIF on a national scale.
source: With the notable exception of South Africa, which has rolled-out Xpert MTB/RIF on a national scale and accounts for almost 50% of global Xpert MTB/RIF volumes, other countries are still reliant on insensitive smears (FIND et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to FIND et al., 2015.

claim: Most high burden countries other than South Africa are still reliant on insensitive smears.
source: With the notable exception of South Africa, which has rolled-out Xpert MTB/RIF on a national scale and accounts for almost 50% of global Xpert MTB/RIF volumes, other countries are still reliant on insensitive smears (FIND et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to FIND et al., 2015.

claim: In 2014, the ratio of smear volumes to Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges procured in South Africa was 1.6.
source: In 2014, the ratio in South Africa was 1.6 – significantly lower than most other high burden countries, where approximately 40–70 smears were performed for each Xpert MTB/RIF test (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qin et al., 2015 providing comparative data.

claim: In 2014, approximately 40-70 smears were performed for each Xpert MTB/RIF test in most high burden countries other than South Africa.
source: In 2014, the ratio in South Africa was 1.6 – significantly lower than most other high burden countries, where approximately 40–70 smears were performed for each Xpert MTB/RIF test (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qin et al., 2015 providing comparative data.

claim: Smears still dominate the TB testing landscape in high burden countries as of 2015.
source: Although the ratio has become more favorable to Xpert MTB/RIF in 2015, smears still dominate the TB testing landscape in high burden countries (Danielle Cazabon, personal communication).
evidence: Supported by personal communication from Danielle Cazabon.

claim: As of 31 December 2016, a total of 6,659 GeneXpert instruments (comprising 29,865 modules) had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing.
source: As of 31 December 2016, a total of 6,659 GeneXpert instruments (comprising 29,865 modules) and 23,140,350 Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing. Source: Cepheid & WHO (World Health Organization, 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 caption and supported by WHO citation from 2017a.

claim: As of 31 December 2016, a total of 23,140,350 Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing.
source: As of 31 December 2016, a total of 6,659 GeneXpert instruments (comprising 29,865 modules) and 23,140,350 Xpert MTB/RIF cartridges had been procured in the public sector in 130 of the 145 countries eligible for concessional pricing. Source: Cepheid & WHO (World Health Organization, 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 caption and supported by WHO citation from 2017a.

claim: Only eight countries have made Xpert MTB/RIF the initial diagnostic test for all people suspected of having TB.
source: From a policy perspective, only eight countries have made Xpert MTB/RIF the initial diagnostic test for all people suspected of having TB, despite the high accuracy of the test and its ability to rapidly detect drug resistance (Albert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albert et al., 2016.

claim: Xpert MTB/RIF has high accuracy.
source: From a policy perspective, only eight countries have made Xpert MTB/RIF the initial diagnostic test for all people suspected of having TB, despite the high accuracy of the test and its ability to rapidly detect drug resistance (Albert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of the test, supported by citation to Albert et al., 2016.

claim: Xpert MTB/RIF has the ability to rapidly detect drug resistance.
source: From a policy perspective, only eight countries have made Xpert MTB/RIF the initial diagnostic test for all people suspected of having TB, despite the high accuracy of the test and its ability to rapidly detect drug resistance (Albert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of the test, supported by citation to Albert et al., 2016.

claim: Only 4% of TB/HIV co-infected patients were actually tested using Xpert MTB/RIF in a recent large, international study in 18 countries.
source: A recent large, international study of Xpert MTB/RIF access and utilization in 18 countries found that the majority of sites had access to Xpert MTB/RIF, but only 4% of TB/HIV co-infected patients were actually tested using Xpert MTB/RIF (Clouse et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clouse et al., 2017 providing study data.

claim: The majority of sites in 18 countries studied had access to Xpert MTB/RIF.
source: A recent large, international study of Xpert MTB/RIF access and utilization in 18 countries found that the majority of sites had access to Xpert MTB/RIF, but only 4% of TB/HIV co-infected patients were actually tested using Xpert MTB/RIF (Clouse et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clouse et al., 2017 providing study data.

claim: Lack of diagnostics with high sensitivity and inadequate access to drug-susceptibility testing forces patients to make multiple visits and spend a lot of money, and increases morbidity.
source: Lack of diagnostics with high sensitivity, and inadequate access to drug-susceptibility testing forces patients to make multiple visits and spend a lot of money, and increases morbidity (Chavan, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chavan, 2017.

claim: Xpert has been endorsed by WHO for use in children.
source: Although tools like Xpert have been endorsed for use in children (World Health Organization, 2013a), and Xpert has been shown to greatly improve the detection of MDR-TB in children (Raizada et al., 2014), access remains a concern in this subgroup.
evidence: Supported by WHO citation from 2013a.

claim: Xpert has been shown to greatly improve the detection of MDR-TB in children.
source: Although tools like Xpert have been endorsed for use in children (World Health Organization, 2013a), and Xpert has been shown to greatly improve the detection of MDR-TB in children (Raizada et al., 2014), access remains a concern in this subgroup.
evidence: Supported by citation to Raizada et al., 2014.

claim: Access to Xpert remains a concern for children.
source: Although tools like Xpert have been endorsed for use in children (World Health Organization, 2013a), and Xpert has been shown to greatly improve the detection of MDR-TB in children (Raizada et al., 2014), access remains a concern in this subgroup.
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion about access issues.

claim: The roll-out of Xpert MTB/RIF has highlighted major implementation gaps that have constrained scale-up of this technology and limited its impact on patient outcomes.
source: As reviewed by Albert and colleagues (Albert et al., 2016), the roll-out of Xpert MTB/RIF has highlighted major implementation gaps that have constrained scale-up of this technology and limited its impact on patient outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Albert et al., 2016.

claim: The roll-out of Xpert MTB/RIF has been hampered by high costs for cash-starved national TB control programs in high-burden countries.
source: The roll-out has been hampered by high costs for cash-starved national TB control programs in high-burden countries.
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion about implementation barriers.

claim: Xpert MTB/RIF identifies more patients with drug-resistance than conventional testing.
source: It is not just the cost of testing, but also the cost of treating MDR-TB, since Xpert MTB/RIF invariably identifies more patients with drug-resistance than conventional testing.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of the test based on its superior sensitivity for drug resistance detection.

claim: A lack of a complete diagnostic package for TB has been a barrier for scale-up of Xpert MTB/RIF.
source: Another barrier for scale-up of Xpert MTB/RIF has been a lack of a complete diagnostic package for TB that includes comprehensive training, quality assurance, implementation plans, and maintenance support (Albert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albert et al., 2016.

claim: Pragmatic trials have shown that the clinical impact of Xpert has been blunted by weak health systems.
source: Also, pragmatic trials have shown that the clinical impact of Xpert has been blunted by weak health systems, resulting in prolonged time to diagnosis and treatment, compounded by empirical therapy by healthcare providers (Theron et al., 2014; Durovni et al., 2014; Churchyard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Theron et al., 2014; Durovni et al., 2014; Churchyard et al., 2015.

claim: Weak health systems result in prolonged time to diagnosis and treatment with Xpert.
source: Also, pragmatic trials have shown that the clinical impact of Xpert has been blunted by weak health systems, resulting in prolonged time to diagnosis and treatment, compounded by empirical therapy by healthcare providers (Theron et al., 2014; Durovni et al., 2014; Churchyard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Theron et al., 2014; Durovni et al., 2014; Churchyard et al., 2015.

claim: In India, an average TB patient is diagnosed after a delay of nearly two months.
source: In India, for example, an average TB patient is diagnosed after a delay of nearly two months and after seeing three providers (Sreeramareddy et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sreeramareddy et al., 2014.

claim: In India, an average TB patient sees three providers before diagnosis.
source: In India, for example, an average TB patient is diagnosed after a delay of nearly two months and after seeing three providers (Sreeramareddy et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sreeramareddy et al., 2014.

claim: Diagnosis is a major gap in the cascade of care in the public sector in India.
source: and diagnosis is a major gap in the cascade of care in the public sector (Subbaraman et al., 2016) and the private sector (Das et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Subbaraman et al., 2016.

claim: Diagnosis is a major gap in the cascade of care in the private sector in India.
source: and diagnosis is a major gap in the cascade of care in the public sector (Subbaraman et al., 2016) and the private sector (Das et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2015.

claim: In South Africa, Xpert MTB/RIF and line probe assays are freely available in centralized laboratories.
source: In South Africa, even though Xpert MTB/RIF and line probe assays are freely available in centralized laboratories, studies show long delays between sample collection and initiation of TB treatment (Hanrahan et al., 2012; Naidoo et al., 2014), and missed opportunities to deploy tests that are available (Chihota et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion about test availability in South Africa.

claim: In South Africa, studies show long delays between sample collection and initiation of TB treatment.
source: In South Africa, even though Xpert MTB/RIF and line probe assays are freely available in centralized laboratories, studies show long delays between sample collection and initiation of TB treatment (Hanrahan et al., 2012; Naidoo et al., 2014), and missed opportunities to deploy tests that are available (Chihota et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanrahan et al., 2012; Naidoo et al., 2014.

claim: In South Africa, there are missed opportunities to deploy tests that are available.
source: In South Africa, even though Xpert MTB/RIF and line probe assays are freely available in centralized laboratories, studies show long delays between sample collection and initiation of TB treatment (Hanrahan et al., 2012; Naidoo et al., 2014), and missed opportunities to deploy tests that are available (Chihota et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chihota et al., 2015.

claim: The private sector has been excluded from concessional Xpert MTB/RIF pricing.
source: In many countries the private sector plays a dominant role in care provision, yet this sector has been excluded from concessional Xpert MTB/RIF pricing, resulting in high costs for patients who pay an average price of nearly USD 70 for the test (Puri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion about pricing policy.

claim: Patients in the private sector pay an average price of nearly USD 70 for the Xpert MTB/RIF test.
source: In many countries the private sector plays a dominant role in care provision, yet this sector has been excluded from concessional Xpert MTB/RIF pricing, resulting in high costs for patients who pay an average price of nearly USD 70 for the test (Puri et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Puri et al., 2016.

claim: Quality of TB care, especially diagnosis, is a concern in the private sector.
source: In addition, quality of TB care, especially diagnosis, is a concern in the private sector (Das et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2015.

claim: Many low-income countries are heavily reliant on external donor funding for TB control.
source: In many countries, TB control receives limited domestic funding, and many low-income countries are heavily reliant on external donor funding (Floyd et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Floyd et al., 2013.

claim: India's governmental expenditure on health is 1.4% of GDP.
source: Despite having the largest number of TB patients in the world, the country's governmental expenditure on health is one of the lowest in the world at 1.4% of GDP (The Lancet, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to The Lancet, 2017.

claim: India has the largest number of TB patients in the world.
source: Despite having the largest number of TB patients in the world, the country's governmental expenditure on health is one of the lowest in the world at 1.4% of GDP (The Lancet, 2017).

claim: India's governmental expenditure on health is one of the lowest in the world.

claim: India's Revised National Tuberculosis Control Program (RNTCP) has struggled to receive budgets necessary to tackle the world's biggest TB epidemic.
source: This under-investment is reflected in India's Revised National Tuberculosis Control Program (RNTCP), which has struggled to receive budgets necessary to tackle the world's biggest TB epidemic (Pai et al., 2017).

source: Although over 600 GeneXpert systems are now available in the Indian public sector, and have been shown to dramatically increase the MDR-TB case detection rates (Sachdeva et al., 2015), the country has restricted the use of this technology primarily to individuals at risk of MDR-TB, persons with TB/HIV co-infection, and children.

claim: GeneXpert systems in India have been shown to dramatically increase the MDR-TB case detection rates.

evidence: This is stated as a factual assertion about India's policy.

claim: India has a new, ambitious plan to eliminate TB by 2025.

claim: It is unclear whether India's TB control budget will match the ambition of the 2025 elimination plan.

claim: Delamanid is a new therapeutic agent for the treatment of MDR-TB introduced in the past five years.
source: The past five years have been a period of great potential with the introduction of two new therapeutic agents for the treatment of MDR-TB: delamanid (Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co, Tokyo, Japan) and bedaquiline (Janssen Therapeutics, NJ, USA) (Gler et al., 2012; Diacon et al., 2014; Field et al., 2012).

claim: Bedaquiline is a new therapeutic agent for the treatment of MDR-TB introduced in the past five years.

claim: Both delamanid and bedaquiline have been conditionally approved by stringent regulatory authorities.

claim: Delamanid and bedaquiline were approved using phase IIB data.

claim: The use of delamanid and bedaquiline was recommended in a cautious way.
